entries.title: The Best James Baldwin Books, recommended by Ahmed Honeini
entries.summary: James Baldwin was a hugely influential figure in 20th-century writing – "one of the foremost American authors of his generation" – explains the literary scholar Ahmed Honeini, as he offers an overview of Baldwin's remarkably varied output, which comprises "extraordinarily creative" fiction and playwriting as well as a body of searing social commentary. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
Thank you for joining us on Five Books to discuss the work of James Baldwin. Could you begin by introducing us to Baldwin: who he was, and why we should continue to read him today?

A pleasure to be here. Baldwin is, without doubt, one of the foremost American authors of his generation. His life and work are fascinating because he not only produced an extraordinary body of creative fiction – like Go Tell It on the Mountain or Giovanni’s Room – but he was also one of the ‘chief chroniclers’ of mid-to-late twentieth-century arts, politics, and society, as his non-fiction and book-length essays such as Notes of a Native Son and The Fire Next Time make clear.

He was at the forefront of the Civil Rights movement, being a friend and fellow-traveller of such pioneering figures as Martin Luther King, Malcolm X, Medgar Evers, Maya Angelou, and Nikki Giovanni, and he was oftentimes called upon by both the media and institutions like Oxford and Cambridge to engage with “the race question” in the United States during the 1950s and 1960s.

Purely from a historical perspective, Baldwin is a wildly influential figure worth remembering, and he just so happens to also be a gorgeously evocative writer, responsible for some of the most poetic and perceptive books ever written. His literary, political, and cultural legacy is immense.

How did you make your selection—what factors did you take into consideration when creating your reading list?

Given how prolific Baldwin’s career and output were, I wanted to be as broad and inclusive as possible. I wanted to offer examples of the best his fiction has to offer, while also foregrounding the quality of his dramatic endeavours and the importance of the theatre in his development as an individual and as an artist, plus making clear that his role as social commentator simply cannot be ignored.

I also wanted to give readers an example of the kinds of writing that Baldwin’s legacy has inspired and generated. Baldwin has had a rich afterlife in the scholarly and biographical community. There have been countless academic monographs and edited essay collections published on him, plus an entire journal – the James Baldwin Review, established in 2015 – dedicated to him. So I wanted to strike a balance between, on the one hand, having Baldwin’s work speak for itself, a point that Baldwin was insistent upon throughout his life, while, on the other hand, making clear that his work has been part of wider critical debates since his death in 1987.

We haven’t forgotten about him.

There are a few notable omissions from your reading list. I suppose I expected you to select Giovanni’s Room, Notes of a Native Son and Another Country… Would you mind addressing that?

Certainly. Giovanni’s Room is widely acknowledged as his masterpiece, while Another Country was one of the most widely-read of his novels during his lifetime. Anybody approaching Baldwin is sure to have read one or both of these books, such that their inclusion in a list like this borders on passé.

Giovanni’s Room, in particular, is noteworthy for being an extraordinarily honest and frank depiction queerness written and published during a moment in history where homosexuality was legally outlawed and socially stigmatized. That novel deserves a whole feature unto itself, such that any remarks I can make here will barely scratch the surface. Notes of a Native Son is accounted for in my selection, albeit discreetly, and I’ll be a little more explicit how later.

Sure, thank you. So let’s talk now about Go Tell It on the Mountain, which was published in 1953. It’s set in 1930s Harlem. 

Go Tell It on the Mountain is Baldwin’s first novel and is, to me, the perfect introduction to his work. I read the novel for the first time when I was studying civil rights history at A-Level when I was around eighteen; my teacher thought that reading a work of fiction alongside studying the racial history and politics of the time would enrich our understanding of the period, and she was absolutely right.

The novel takes place primarily on the birthday of its protagonist, fourteen-year-old preacher John Grimes, and is based closely upon Baldwin’s own childhood. Baldwin, in painstaking and exquisite detail, foregrounds John’s experiences within his church, the Temple of the Fire Baptized; his contentious relationship with his family, especially his father; his efforts to reconcile his burgeoning queerness with his religious upbringing, and the fear and shame that emerges as a result.

In amidst John’s personal history, Baldwin weaves in and out of the present day of 1930s Harlem, focusing on the past of Elizabeth and Gabriel, John’s mother and father, and the lingering ambiguities surrounding John’s parentage. The experience of actually reading the novel belies any attempt I can make to do a proper introduction justice, so let me stop there.

Go Tell It on the Mountain features hallucinatory religious visions; Baldwin himself was preaching in a Pentecostal church at 13. How does this religious or spiritual intensity manifest across his career?

Undoubtedly so, and the question of Baldwin’s religiosity – or lack thereof – continues to preoccupy readers and critics of his life and work.

Go Tell It on the Mountain makes explicitly clear the importance of the Pentecostal-Holiness Church tradition upon Baldwin, a tradition that he rejected and rebelled against when left the church when he turned 17. Baldwin tried to articulate his ambivalence towards organised religion many times during his career, and I think his efforts are best summarised in The Fire Next Time, where he asserts:

It is not too much to say that whoever wishes to become a truly moral human being […] must first divorce himself from all the prohibitions, crimes, and hypocrisies of the Christian church. If the concept of God has any validity or any use, it can only be to make us larger, freer, and more loving. If God cannot do this, then it is time we got rid of Him.

It’s very powerful.

There is a palpable sense of feeling towards the Church, towards God, that Baldwin repeatedly circles in his life and throughout his writing and that, despite his anger, never fully stops contemplating or makes a clean break from. As Douglas Field argues, we need to understand “how his work diverges from, and resonates with, aspects of Pentecostalism, rather than simply labelling Baldwin as secular or irreligious.”

I agree with Field entirely. Saying that Baldwin was merely an apostate is much too neat, especially when the spectre of the Church and of Christianity appears in his writings long after he enters adulthood.

Let’s stay on topic with The Amen Corner, his 1954 play. It features a church pastor who, it transpires, left her husband to pursue a religious life. Would you tell us more?

The Amen Corner was written immediately after Go Tell It on the Mountain and, as Baldwin himself acknowledges in his introduction to the published script,

Writing [the play] I remember as a desperate and even rather irresponsible act—it was certainly considered irresponsible by my agent at that time. She did not wish to discourage me, but it was her duty to let me know that the American theatre was not exactly clamoring for plays on obscure aspects of Negro life, especially one written by a virtually unknown author whose principal effort until that time had been one novel.

The reason why Baldwin felt compelled to write the play, however, is two-fold, first because of the centrality of the theatre to his early life and, second because of his experiences in the Church, experiences that were first represented in Go Tell It.

As he outlines in The Devil Finds Work, Baldwin was taken to the theatre regularly by his elementary school teacher; he vividly recounts having seen Orson Welles’s Macbeth at the Lafyette Theatre in Harlem in 1936, a legendary production featuring a cast of exclusively Black and African American actors. Seeing that production was one of the formative cultural experiences that Baldwin experienced during his early life.

Crucially, Baldwin discovers the theatre at the same moment when he begins to realise, as he writes in his introduction to The Amen Corner, “the fact that I was born in the church”:

I knew that out of the ritual of the church, historically speaking, comes the act of theatre, the communion which is the theatre. And I knew what I wanted to do in the theatre was to recreate moments I remembered as a boy preacher, to involve the people, even against their will, to shake them up, and, hopefully, to change them.

Sister Margaret Alexander, the church pastor at the heart of the play, is a wonderfully exuberant figure who does exactly what Baldwin thought that the church-as-theatre should do: she involves her congregation, she shakes them up, and she tries to change them, no matter how forcefully. Yet her attempts at exercising authority over her flock while also denying her personal history renders her position within the church untenable by the play’s end and contributes to her exile.

Why do you see The Amen Corner as one of his best or most significant works?

On one level, The Amen Corner proves, to me, that Baldwin was an extraordinarily versatile craftsman. He could excel within an astonishing range of literary forms – the novel, the short story, the poem, the essay – and The Amen Corner is, without doubt, a wonderful play. On another level, however, Baldwin’s career as a playwright is virtually ignored; so many colleagues and fellow Americanists have no idea he wrote a play, let alone that his second play, Blues for Mister Charlie, had an ill-fated run on Broadway.

So when you consider the centrality of the theatre to Baldwin’s life and development as an artist, when you consider the context in which The Amen Corner was written – in the immediate aftermath of Go Tell It on the Mountain, the novel that launched his career – and when you then realise that Baldwin’s theatrical efforts have long been underappreciated, I think it’s important for his plays, and for The Amen Corner in particular, to have a moment in the sun.

Baldwin, in fact, was working on a play entitled The Welcome Table (which has been staged in the early 1990s by the Academy of the Arts in Philadelphia but which has never been published) immediately prior to his death. The fact that Baldwin was returning to the dramatic form even towards the end of his life proves his love for the theatre, and The Amen Corner as an expression of that love, is difficult to ignore or deny.

Got it. Next, let’s talk about If Beale Street Could Talk, which is a much later novel, released in 1974. In it, a young woman falls in love with a man who has been wrongly accused of rape.

To me, no matter how corny what I am about to say might sound, there is no purer artistic expression of the power of love – regardless of sexuality – than Tish and Fonny’s love in that novel. The novel is littered with innumerable examples of such expressions; taking one example at random, Tish says that she

thought of Fonny’s touch, of Fonny, in my arms, his breath, his touch, his odor, his weight, that terrible and beautiful presence riding into me and his breath being snarled, as if by a golden thread, deeper and deeper in his throat as he rode—as he rode deeper and deeper not so much into me as into a kingdom which lay just behind his eyes. He worked on wood that way. He worked on stone that way. If I had never seen him work, I might never have known he loved me.

Such moments of complete and utter erotic abandon suggest that, to Baldwin, as with a writer like Tennessee Williams, sexuality and emotionality are inextricably linked; sexuality becomes a means through which to express the depthless nature of one’s adoration for another.

Dagmawi Moubshet made an interesting point in The Atlantic: “the novel centers on the emotional bonds holding two African American families together. By contrast, the author had spent the previous decade instead writing and thinking about love as a collective American experience, one whose power came from the fact that it could cut across racial lines.”

I think Moubshet is right to broaden Baldwin’s focus on love beyond Tish and Fonny themselves. Their erotic and emotional relationship exists within a much wider network of familial love, and the novel is profoundly invested in exploring the extraordinary lengths people will go to support those they love when external forces threaten them. The efforts of Tish’s mother, Sharon, to clear Fonny’s name are perhaps the most obvious example.

What is particularly interesting about Beale Street, then, is that Baldwin concentrates this enormous idea of love within the intimate relationships between particular people and families. The fact that Tish’s love for Fonny never diminishes at any point in the novel, even after he is falsely imprisoned for sexual assault, but that their love is sustained and is, in fact, the only means by which they are able to survive the racial and legal injustice they face, effectively proves a point that Baldwin introduces in The Amen Corner, funnily enough: “It’s a awful thing to think about, the way love never dies!”

In other words, Tish and Fonny’s love is the only source of relief and sustenance they get from this awful situation, but paradoxically Fonny’s imprisonment is an awful physical impediment to that love, which is incredibly cruel and ironic, I think.

Next we will talk about two nonfiction books, first Baldwin’s own collected nonfiction The Price of the Ticket. What are the highlights – does it include his famous essays from The Fire Next Time?

Yes, and if you’ll permit me, choosing The Price of the Ticket was kind of a cheat because the volume contains most of Baldwin’s substantive nonfiction, including Notes of a Native Son, Nobody Knows My Name, The Devil Finds Work, and yes, The Fire Next Time. I simply couldn’t bring myself to choose only one of his essay collections, because to do so would diminish or underrepresent just how incisive and persuasive Baldwin’s prowess as a public intellectual was and remains.

Crucially, his essays are as engaging, thought-provoking, and awe-inspiring as his creative work; to me, non-fiction is usually so difficult to recommend to a casual reader unless the author in question is truly adept at the essay form (say Virginia Woolf or Toni Morrison). Baldwin, as I’ve made clear earlier, is just such a writer, because he communicates his ideas with such breathtaking precision and clarity. By far my most highly treasured quotation of his is from No Name in the Street:

People pay for what they do, and, still more, for what they have already allowed themselves to become. And they pay for it very simply: by the lives they lead.

If that doesn’t convince you to pick up Baldwin’s essays, nothing will!

That brings us, finally, to David Leeming’s James Baldwin: A Biography. What do we learn from this that Baldwin does not tell us himself?

Leeming’s biography is interesting because he and Baldwin were close friends. So, unlike biographers like Joseph Blotner (of William Faulkner) or John Lahr (of Joe Orton or Tennessee Williams), who maintained a distance from their subject, Leeming’s work is intended to be an inside view of Baldwin – not salacious, but certainly not superficial, either.

Readers of this particular biography get an acute sense of Baldwin as an author – there are individual chapters dedicated to each of Baldwin’s major works, including, crucially, his plays and screenplay – and Baldwin as a man: his relationships, his public persona, and his temperament. So, as with the best biographies, you get a truly rounded view of the man; you see what makes him tick as a creative artist, but you also see him during moments of… emotional abandon, let’s say, that border on the intense and, at times, even hilarious.

One moment that springs to mind is during the original Broadway production of Blues for Mister Charlie, the rehearsals for which were physically demanding and emotionally heated. Baldwin was having countless issues with the producers, particularly Lee Strasberg, because of the play’s length and because of his insistence that ticket prices be kept affordable for working-class African Americans. Leeming writes that, during one rehearsal session, Baldwin arrived at the theatre “in a towering rage, to which he gave added metaphorical value by climbing an electrician’s ladder” accusing Strasberg of, “among other things, incompetence ‘to the point of sabotage’.” That image of the 5’5” Baldwin, this usually contemplative and poetic figure, getting so up in arms about the ‘incompetence’ of his producers that he scales an electrician’s ladder to give them a piece of his mind is just delicious!

Leeming’s biography set a standard for Baldwin scholarship, and while there have been subsequent, excellent biographies like Mullen’s James Baldwin: Living in Fire or Nicholas Boggs’s Baldwin: A Love Story, Leeming’s book remains the gold standard as far as Baldwin’s life is concerned, I would say.

What has Baldwin’s writing come to mean to you?

As an academic, I’ve long been fascinated by what we call the ‘single-author study,’ a comprehensive scholarly examination of a writer’s body of work. So far, I’ve written two, one on William Faulkner, the other on Tennessee Williams. Any book takes years to write, and so you have to be able to find a subject that you know will sustain your interest for the foreseeable future and keep you in the library or at your desk for hours on end. Baldwin is the third such writer who I’ve decided to take on with a single-author study; I am currently in the early stages of writing my third book, James Baldwin Between Stage and Screen: The Politics of Sacrifice, which looks at Baldwin’s dramatic and cinematic output and what they tell us about the nature of socio-political, religious, and interpersonal sacrifice.

The figures at the heart of my project – Sister Margaret Alexander in The Amen Corner, Richard Henry in Blues for Mister Charlie, and Malcolm X/El Hajj Malik El-Shabazz in One Day When I Was Lost – become vessels through which Baldwin is able to represent the impact that an unshakeable belief in an idea – the Pentecostal Church in Margaret’s case, social injustice in Richard’s, and the Nation of Islam in Malcolm’s – has upon the individual during the civil rights era of the 1950s and 1960s.

I won’t say too much more about the project at this point, other than that I hope the finished book contributes to a resurgence in popular and scholarly attention on Baldwin’s contributions to the theatre and to cinema, which deserve to be celebrated. On a more personal level, I suppose the fact that I’m willing to spend several years of my life thinking and writing about Baldwin is itself an answer to what his work has come to mean to me. I keep finding things in his writing that surprise me, challenge me, move me, or force me to reconsider what I thought I understood about him since first encountering him. After spending several years reading Baldwin, I still don’t feel that I’m finished with him – and, for a scholar, I can think of few greater compliments to pay a writer.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

September 30, 2026

entries.title: The best books on Battles, recommended by Iain MacGregor
entries.summary: The weapons and tactics of war may change, but the human experience of battle does not, argues Iain MacGregor, author of Battle: The Moments that Transformed Warfare from Ancient Greece to Ukraine. He highlights five books that bring that experience to life, from the ordinary soldier at Agincourt to the brutal realities of the Pacific War and the Falklands. This interview appeared first on Five Bo
entries.content:
In your book, you cover a lot of battles in a lot of places over an extremely long period of time. What did you ultimately conclude?

This is my fifth, and as with all the books I’ve written, it’s not exactly the one I started out writing. Generally, I do people- and story-led books, which relates to two or three of my choices that we’re going to talk about.

This was a diversion. Most historians who are in the genre want to do a book like this because it’s almost like exercising your chops. How much do I know? What are the theories behind it? So I always wanted to do it. You don’t get narrowed down to just one war or battle and 3,000 years of history—that’s exciting.

What I discovered was,  the more research I did—whether it was ancient history, medieval, Tudor, Napoleonic, World War Two—that while the tactics and technology have changed radically, the human dimension is always the same. It’s about human beings.

Whether it’s the commanders, or the line officers on the ground, or the soldiers, they’ve all got the same frailties you and I have got. It doesn’t matter whether they’re a Greek hoplite, a Tudor English sailor, or a Ukrainian soldier on the front line today, you’re still scared. It’s about how you react under pressure. If you’re a commander, it’s about the timing, about how you deal with sudden events.

That hasn’t changed ever, and writing this book over this whole timeline really confirmed that to me.

How much research did you do to cover that many periods?

I’ve edited history books for more than three decades, and military history has been a constant thread throughout my career. Some subjects stay with you. Even when I’m not working on a particular project, I’m always collecting material, whether in notebooks, voice memos, or on my laptop. Over the years I’ve built up tens of thousands of notes on battles, commanders and campaigns. So, when I was asked what I wanted to write, I already had a vast reservoir of research to draw on.

That wasn’t the end of it. For this book I read well over a hundred additional works and revisited many of the battlefields themselves. I’ve walked Civil War sites in Virginia, explored battlefields across Britain, and spent time on key locations in Europe, Russia, Vietnam and Japan. There’s no substitute for standing on the ground, seeing the distances, the terrain and the decisions that commanders had to make.

People often ask how I find the time. The truth is that publishing is already all-consuming; I edit twenty or more books a year. But after enough years, you learn to trust the process. Research accumulates steadily, often unnoticed, until one day you realise you’ve spent decades preparing to write the book that was in your head all along.

OK, so you’ve mentioned reading over 100 books, including all the ones you’ve read over the years. How did you choose these particular five? What were your criteria?

Some were whether they affected how I thought history should be told. I’d say front of that cab rank is John Keegan’s The Face of Battle. It’s probably had more of an influence on me than anything else. A couple of these books are seminal, and I would argue that your readers should definitely go out and read them. Others, like, for instance, With the Old Breed, which we’ll talk about by E.B. Sledge, has got the human factor that I just find gripping. It’s just such a brilliant, raw, emotive, visceral book. It’s not even a memoir—it’s almost like he’s taken it as therapy. It really moved me. Then there are other books that shine a light on aspects of big battles people know about, but hadn’t really thought of them in that way.

Let’s go through each of them and tell me about them, bearing in mind that not everyone may have read them. Let’s start with The Face of Battle (1976) by John Keegan, which covers three battles. Tell me a bit more about the book and and and why it’s so seminal.

John Keegan’s The Face of Battle is arguably the most influential work of military history written in the last fifty years. It radically altered the next generation of published historians coming through.

Before Keegan—and I’ve read a lot of books that came out before—it was always about the great people, generally men of military history. You’re looking at warfare or the battle itself from the top down. You learn about the great strategist who might have won or lost the battle, but not what life was like on the front line for the ordinary person doing the fighting. That’s what Keegan brings to it.

He does it by examining three of the most important battles (from a British perspective) you would want to know about: Agincourt in 1415, Waterloo in 1815, and then the Somme in 1916. These are battles that resonate in every household across Great Britain and further afield. Keegan gives you the background and the context, but he captures them from the ordinary person’s perspective.

What I loved about it when I read it in my early twenties was the fact that it was just so accessible. I thought, ‘He’s writing this for me. This is the way I would like to read history.’ I’ve got dozens of books on my shelf that are very important but they’re very dry—whereas he’s bringing it to life. I mean, in the process of writing my new book, I must have gone back to John’s book at least ten times, because it’s just so good. It’s like a breath of fresh air. I read it again just to get inspired.

With a medieval battle like Agincourt, how do you get the on-the-ground view? There must be a lot more information about the leaders.

With the leaders, you’ve got a lot of material from the time. Then, maybe decades afterwards, you can read about the commanders of the period on both sides, and records showing the casualties.

It’s not that the first-hand material is super scant, but if there’s not much around, you then spread the net slightly wider, and you look at other key battles in the period and how the fighting has been recorded. It’s completely accurate and fair to then add that to whatever work you’re doing.

He’s obviously gone to these places. He’s giving you a bird’s-eye view of the terrain and the weather and what the terrain would be like in that weather.

It gives you an insider’s idea and appreciation of what they were facing. How ferocious was the fighting? Did the tactics work? Did they fail? Was the weather that big of a factor? Was the longbow that big a factor? He brings it to the page in the way that someone like Bernard Cornwell would do in fiction. He really brings it alive, and you want to find out what’s happened to this person he’s writing about, or that unit. That’s what I’ve always found captivating.

One of my colleagues interviewed Antony Beevor about World War Two. She asked him which historian inspired him, and he also mentioned John Keegan, The Face of Battle.

I think if you interviewed any current military historian/author right now, they would say the same thing. There’s no argument. It’s a seminal book. It came out decades ago, but it’s still very much in print.

Let’s turn to your next choice, The Killer Angels (1974) by Michael Shaara. This is set during the American Civil War, and it is actually a novel, is that right?

Yes, it is, but I definitely wanted to bring it in because it’s had just as big of an effect on me as John Keegan’s work has. I am a huge American Civil War researcher and author. I’ve been to quite a few of the battlegrounds in the eastern theatre in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. I’ve even written a book about it, U.S. Civil War: Battle by Battle.

The Killer Angels is perfect in that Michael Shaara takes Gettysburg, the pivotal battle of the American Civil War, if not in modern American military history, and brings it to life. You can tell he’s done the research because of the way he talks about the units on the move and the planning. The fighting itself at Gettysburg is very, very accurate. The man’s done his homework, but he’s just got that fictional writer’s skill. He just brings to life the drama of the human experience.

You can understand why countless Hollywood producers and directors have read The Killer Angels. At the same time, they’re reading nonfiction books that enable them to picture whatever scene they want to: whether it’s the first, second, or final day of fighting at Gettysburg in July 1863, such as ‘Pickett’s Charge’.

That’s why I think the book is important. You need someone like Michael Shaara because he takes what you might think of as, ‘oh, it’s just military history ’ and he opens it up to a much wider audience. He pulls in a general readership to then study what you could argue are serious nonfiction works about Gettysburg and the wider American Civil War. So, it works on lots of levels.

I was just reading the beginning about the scout checking out where the troops are. It’s very gripping, isn’t it?

Yes. Also, as an editor, what I liked about the book is that he avoids caricatures. He’s writing about the people, the main participants, but he’s not throwing a big bucket of clichés on them. That makes it more believable.

Let’s go to the next book about a battle, which takes us to World War I and Verdun. This is a big favourite in our family. What can you tell me about The Price of Glory (1962) by Alistair Horne?

I’m a recent convert. I was a history lecturer and guide on a cruise around Japan and South Korea in June. I was giving quite a few lectures on Japanese history, which made me realise I wanted to read something that completely took me away from that area, so I could relax. I bought The Price of Glory—I told you I was a military history geek! I thought l’d be having too much of a good time to read the book properly, but I did. I read it cover to cover in six nights.

Can you say a bit about the Battle of Verdun for those who may not be as familiar with it?

The Battle of Verdun was a ten-month-long ordeal in which France and Germany sacrificed hundreds of thousands of men for a few miles of devastated ground. It’s why the Battle of the Somme was necessary to the north, as we, the British, were trying to relieve the pressure on Verdun, which lay to the southeast of our own trenchlines.

Verdun was more than a battlefield. For France, it was a symbol of national survival: a ring of great forts strung across the landscape, long regarded as impregnable. Far from the fighting in Belgium, the sector had been relatively quiet, which was precisely why the Germans chose it. Their aim was not simply to seize ground, but to destroy France’s will to continue the war. As one German commander put it, they would ‘bleed France white’.

The battle opened on 21 February 1916 with one of the heaviest bombardments the world had yet seen. Around a million shells crashed onto French positions on the first day alone. For weeks the Germans seemed unstoppable. Fort after fort came under attack, French units were hurled into the line and shattered by artillery fire, and Verdun became an industrialised slaughterhouse on a scale scarcely imaginable. By the spring of 1916, it appeared possible that the Germans might break through altogether.

Yet Verdun produced the opposite result from the one Berlin expected. Instead of crushing French morale, it hardened it. The battle became a rallying cry for a nation under siege, a test of endurance that France refused to fail. Like the Somme in British memory, Verdun is remembered for its terrible losses, but in France it also carries the meaning of sacrifice, resilience and national defiance. It remains, perhaps more than any other battlefield, part of the military soul of the nation.

In The Price of Glory, Alistair Horne really brings to the page the ordinary human experience of Verdun. It’s just hell on earth. It’s this dystopian, mad landscape of destruction. And I think if John Keegan, in The Face of War, explains what battle feels like, this book explains how entire societies are pulled in to try and win what looks like a hopeless situation. Because that’s what happens. It’s what happens with the Soviet Union at Stalingrad in the Second World War. You manage to rouse the nation by declaring, ‘This is an existential threat. We could lose the country and be overrun if we are defeated.’

Verdun is, I think, the turning point for France. It saved the country in the Great War.

Let’s go on to the Pacific in World War II now, and you’ve chosen a memoir. This is With the Old Breed by E.B. Sledge.

This book is captured in the TV series The Pacific. It’s the Pacific version of Band of Brothers. A few years ago, I wrote a book called The Hiroshima Men, about the war in the Pacific and the race for the atomic bomb. To explain to my readers why you would drop an atom bomb on a city of human beings, I chart the progress of the war over three years and showcase how brutal it was – for the military as well as civilians. There was no quarter given, and no weapon off the table for either side.

The main character in the HBO series, Eugene Sledge, was a young U.S. Marine who doesn’t even enter the fighting until September 1944, but he’s then in some of the most vicious combat as American naval forces ‘island hop’ through the South and Central Pacific to establish bases close enough to bomb Japanese cities and ultimately invade the country. Equally, Japan knows that they must not allow this to happen or it will be unconditional surrender. That’s where the ferocity of their defence turns suicidal and casualties mount on both sides. American forces lost more men in the final year of the war than in the previous three years combined. That’s where Sledge’s memoir begins.

‘The Old Breed’ is a term given to veteran U.S. Marines, but these young, raw recruits like Sledge soon learn the art of war because of the brutality of the fighting on Okinawa and the fact the veterans already serving in their unit are being killed. It becomes about survival.

What I found emotive and why I chose it is that this book—above most other World War Two memoirs—is just incredible for capturing the psychological damage of being on the front line. It’s visceral. You can see why Tom Hanks’s production company based half the HBO series just on this single piece of biography, because the things Sledge witnesses, the fighting he experiences, his friends dying, the sheer waste of it all are perfectly captured in this memoir.

Sledge couldn’t write it when he came home. He was too damaged. It took him years to distil it, to then be ready to write down his epic tale. Most of the best World War Two memoirs, from an American perspective, started to come out in the mid-1950s because by then they could think, ‘I’m ready to put pen to paper.’ With the Old Breed is the standard against which you’d measure current memoirs. Are they as good as his? Because his is just extraordinary. And who knew? And I think it surprised him too. He’s such a gifted writer.

He went on to become a biology professor, I believe.

I’ve interviewed veterans from the Second World War on all sides in the process of writing my last two books, and there were quite a few who went on to have outstanding, stellar academic careers. There was one who was about to turn 100 when I spoke to him, he’s a professor at Colorado University. He was on Iwo Jima for three weeks and survived. He saw most of his friends killed and he said he jumped for joy when he realised they’d used the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. It took him years to understand just how terrible a decision that was. He said, ‘I regret it now but, at the time, I was 20 and I just wanted to live.’

A few months ago, I interviewed someone whose dad had been on the Burma Railway, and she’d just published his diary. She recommended the E.B. Sledge book as well, but I haven’t read it yet. I’m a bit scared to get to it.

You could watch the HBO series instead. It’s ten episodes and he’s in half of it. I honestly think the series really does capture the book because it’s so visual.

Let’s turn to your last book, A Soldier’s Song (1992) by Ken Lukowiak, which is about the Falklands War.

I was a young teenager when the Falklands War was on. I began my career in publishing in 1992, at a big London-based publisher. It was my first job and my degree was in history. I was surrounded by books and people would say ‘Just take one.’  You think, ‘Wow, it’s like Christmas!’ The publisher I was working for had just published this book.

A Soldier’s Song by Ken Lukowiak tells the story of what it was like to fight and survive down in the Falklands with the British forces. Lukowiak is an elite soldier, serving with 2nd Para. He’s been trained and highly conditioned to kill, and they did. They were very, very effective in the Falklands: arguably the best-performing unit.

It’s a bit like Sledge’s book, With the Old Breed, in that Lukowiak is adept at describing the fighting. But then it becomes almost like a novel from the 1960s where you’re finding the tragicomedy from Vietnam. Lukowiak’s candour and his humour are allied with emotional intelligence.

It paints a picture of what it’s like to switch from being bored for days on end because nothing’s happening, and then all of a sudden—bam!—you’re in the thick of the fighting. Bullets are flying around you in the dark and there is tracer fire everywhere. Your friends are dropping left and right. He captures that effectively, which is surprising because he’s not a trained writer, he’s a squaddie. Also, like Sledge, he wrote it years after the event. It’s about having the ability to put your mind back to that period you probably don’t want to revisit and bring it back to life.

At the time, I don’t think A Soldier’s Song was a bestseller. I have mentioned it a few times to people over the years, and they don’t know it. It’s still available secondhand on Amazon. It’s fantastic, and I’ve still got a copy that’s 30 years old at least. I see it as one of the most important books on the British side to come out of the Falklands campaign because, again, in a Keeganesque way, it’s talking about the ordinary soldier’s experience.

I haven’t read any books about the Falklands, and like you, I was pretty young at the time. What’s the story he’s telling?

The Falklands War began when Argentina’s military junta seized the islands in April 1982. Margaret Thatcher’s government rejected any suggestion of accepting the occupation and instead dispatched a naval task force to retake them. At the heart of the campaign were units such as the Royal Marines, the Parachute Regiment and the Guards, who faced the formidable task of advancing across difficult terrain towards Port Stanley.

Among them was Vincent Bramley Lukowiak of 2 Para, a battalion that found itself confronting well-armed Argentine forces entrenched on the high ground surrounding the capital. The British landed far from the main Argentine positions and had to march for days across bleak, windswept ground before assaulting a series of heavily defended objectives. The odds were often daunting, and while the British eventually prevailed, the victories came at a cost.

What makes Lukowiak’s memoir so powerful is that it strips away the patriotic headlines and triumphalism that followed the war. He takes the reader onto the battlefield itself: the freezing rain, the sodden peat bogs, the exhaustion, fear and uncertainty of combat. His story is not simply about military success, but about the human experience of war and the lasting physical and psychological burden carried by those who fought it.
